questions.solution: Shape d (blue capital letter T) has \(1\) line of symmetry.

questions.solution: Shape B covers \(9 + 1 + 2 = 12\) squares and Shape D covers \(3 \times 4 = 12\) squares, so B and D have the same area.

questions.hint: Multiply the number of rows by the number of columns for each rectangle and find the pair where both products equal 12.

keyPoints.text: different shapes that cover the same area
keyPoints.note: Two different rectangles have the same area if rows × columns gives the same number of squares.

questions.solution: A \(3 \times 4\) rectangle covers \(12\) squares and a \(2 \times 6\) rectangle also covers \(12\) squares.

steps.explain: To find the area of a rectangle on grid paper, multiply the number of rows by the number of columns.

questions.stem: Use Base 10 flats, exercise books or envelopes to measure the area of your desk. Since a Base 10 flat is smaller than an exercise book, how will the number of Base 10 flats needed to cover the desk compare to the number of exercise books?

options: More Base 10 flats than exercise books are needed because each flat has a smaller area.
Fewer Base 10 flats than exercise books are needed because each flat has a smaller area.
The exact same number of Base 10 flats and exercise books are needed to cover the desk.
Fewer Base 10 flats than exercise books are needed because each book has a smaller area.
questions.hint: Think about covering the same desk: does a smaller tile take more pieces or fewer pieces to cover the same surface?

keyPoints.text: Base 10 flats, exercise books or envelopes to measure the area of your desk
keyPoints.note: Smaller measuring units require a larger number of units to cover the same area.

questions.solution: Because a Base 10 flat has a smaller area than an exercise book, it takes more Base 10 flats than exercise books to cover the same desk.

steps.explain: Compare the size of the two units: a Base 10 flat (\(10\text{ cm} \times 10\text{ cm}\)) is much smaller than an exercise book.

options: Rectangular units fit together edge-to-edge without leaving gaps or overlaps.
Rectangular units leave large circular gaps between them that are easy to count.
Different-sized rectangular units can be mixed together in the same area count.
Overlapping the rectangular units on top of each other gives the exact area.
questions.hint: Look at how the rectangular books/flats sit next to one another on the desk top.

keyPoints.text: most suitable for measuring the desk
keyPoints.note: Good area units must be uniform in size and tile (fit together) without gaps or overlaps.

questions.solution: Rectangular units (such as exercise books, envelopes, or Base 10 flats) are suitable because their straight edges fit together edge-to-edge with no gaps and no overlaps.

steps.explain: Look at the rectangular units arranged across the rectangular desk surface.

questions.stem: Jacqui covered her desk with round ice-cream lids. Do you think these are good measuring units for area, and why?

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 340 145" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="50%" height="auto" style="max-width:340px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="0" y="0" width="340" height="145" rx="8" fill="#ffffff"/><line x1="56" y1="84" x2="56" y2="132" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><line x1="256" y1="84" x2="256" y2="132" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><line x1="96" y1="68" x2="96" y2="108" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3.5"/><line x1="296" y1="54" x2="296" y2="108" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="4"/><polygon points="50,84 96,34 300,34 254,84" fill="#bae6fd" stroke="#1e293b" stroke-width="1.8"/><ellipse cx="104" cy="48" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="48" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="196" cy="48" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="242" cy="48" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="86" cy="70" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="132" cy="70" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="178" cy="70" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/><ellipse cx="224" cy="70" rx="20" ry="9" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

options: Yes, because circular lids are much easier to trace around than square tiles.
No, because round lids cannot fit together without leaving gaps between them.
Yes, because the uncovered gaps between the round lids do not have any area.
No, because round lids are too heavy to place flat on top of a student desk.
questions.hint: Look closely at the spaces between the round ice-cream lids on Jacqui’s desk.

keyPoints.text: round ice-cream lids
keyPoints.note: Circles have curved edges, so placing them side by side always leaves uncovered spaces (gaps) in between.

questions.solution: No, round ice-cream lids are not good measuring units for area because curved circles leave uncovered gaps between them.

steps.explain: Look at Jacqui’s desk covered with round ice-cream lids.
steps.work: \(\text{Inspect the round lids on the desk}\)
